title: What is the Bechdel Test?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explain the Bechdel Test, using Casablanca as a worked example. They cover its origin in Alison Bechdel's 1985 Dykes to Watch Out For strip (credited to Liz Wallace), the test's two rules, and its spread online in the 2000s. They review statistics on women's speaking roles and on films and Best Picture nominees that pass or fail, with examples like Jackie Brown, Avatar, Gravity, Weird Science and Guardians of the Galaxy. They discuss criticism of the test (Martha Lauzen), alternatives like the Mako Mori test and the sexy lamp test, Geena Davis's gender-in-media work, FiveThirtyEight's 2017 campaign, behind-the-camera representation, and ways audiences can respond. The episode opens with a plug for The Bechdel Cast and closes with a tribute to Gordon Lightfoot in place of listener mail.
topics: Geena Davis Institute on Gender in Media

segments.title: Opening and credits
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, credit their sources, and plug The Bechdel Cast, a sister podcast on the iHeart network.

segments.title: Casablanca example and women's speaking roles
segments.summary: Using Casablanca, the hosts show how it has no conversation between two women. They cite USC Annenberg figures that about 67 percent of speaking roles in top 2018 films went to men and describe how bit parts and crowd scenes are mostly male.

segments.title: Origin and rules of the Bechdel Test
segments.summary: The test comes from Alison Bechdel's 1985 Dykes to Watch Out For strip, credited to friend Liz Wallace, and spread online in the 2000s. The hosts explain the rules: two named women who talk to each other about something other than a man. They also mention Virginia Woolf's observation about women in fiction.

segments.title: Whether podcasts can fail the test
segments.summary: The hosts joke about whether their own two-man podcast would fail and note that critics say the test is imperfect.

segments.title: Pass and fail rates in films and Best Picture winners
segments.summary: About 70 percent of AFI's top 100 American films from 1916 to 2001 fail the test. Thor: Ragnarok fails despite strong female characters. A 2018 BBC study found fewer than half of Best Picture winners pass, while most recent winners do.

segments.title: Nominees and debate over passing
segments.summary: Chuck lists recent Best Picture nominees that fail, including Joker and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and some that pass. The hosts say the test is meant to be debated and that passing depends on the quality of the conversation.
topics: Once Upon a Time in Hollywood

segments.title: Examples that pass or fail
segments.summary: Jackie Brown fails though it has a strong female lead, and Chuck notes a film failing does not make it bad. Goodfellas and American Pie 2 pass. Weird Science and Showgirls also pass. Avatar and Gravity fail despite strong female characters.

segments.title: Rear Window, Guardians of the Galaxy and more examples
segments.summary: Rear Window passes with Grace Kelly and Thelma Ritter working together. Guardians of the Galaxy passes through Gamora and Nebula's relationship. The hosts discuss Hitchcock's off-screen behavior and the value of films regardless of the test result.

segments.title: Historical context and critiques of the test
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1985 context and feminist waves, with Chuck pushing back on the idea that the 1980s lacked women-led films. They cite Martha Lauzen's criticism that the test is too low a bar and that it misses sexualized portrayals.

segments.title: Stalking, older actresses and Geena Davis
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the portrayal of sexual assault and stalking in films, the difficulty older women face getting roles, and Geena Davis's institute and her 2012 Rutgers talk on gender in media.
topics: Geena Davis Institute on Gender in Media

segments.title: Geena Davis anecdotes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck share anecdotes about Geena Davis's personality and reputation on set.

segments.title: FiveThirtyEight campaign and behind-the-camera diversity
segments.summary: In 2017 FiveThirtyEight asked a dozen women in the industry for alternatives to the test, including Lena Waithe and Rooney Mara's counterpart Rory Uphold's suggestion of 50 percent women film crews. The hosts describe gender gaps in film departments and the four categories of suggestions.

segments.title: Women directors and alternative tests
segments.summary: Female directors are linked to higher female speaking roles. The hosts cover the Mako Mori test and the sexy lamp test, and suggest ways audiences can respond, such as avoiding films or Swedish cinemas rating films by gender bias.

segments.title: 2022 statistics on top-grossing films
segments.summary: USC Annenberg data shows 9 percent of the top 100 films of 2022 were directed by women and 2.7 percent by women of color. Independent films are more likely to pass. The hosts note that movies shape how kids see reality.

segments.title: TV versus film
segments.summary: The hosts say TV has historically done better than movies on female-centric shows, naming One Day at a Time, Alice, and The Carol Burnett Show.

segments.title: Tribute to Gordon Lightfoot in place of listener mail
segments.summary: No listener mail this episode. The hosts mark the death of Gordon Lightfoot and mention an upcoming Canadian show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck invites listener mail at the show's email address, and Josh gives the iHeartRadio production credit.
